claims.text: As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films and nanoribbons have substantial residual lattice strain, defects, and defect-rich interfaces.
The enhanced surface, defect, and residual-strain density in these low-dimensional alloys increases magnetic domain-wall pinning.
Increased domain-wall pinning suppresses the effective magnetocaloric response under low applied fields.
Increased domain-wall pinning enhances magnetic hysteresis during low-field cooling cycles.
Residual strain and nanoscale defects blur the magnetic phase transition through domain-wall pinning.
Controlled post-deposition annealing can partially relieve residual lattice strain without fully crystallizing the material.
Controlled annealing modifies the density of defects and interfaces that act as pinning centers.
Partial strain relief and defect modification reduce magnetic domain-wall pinning.
Reduced pinning permits a more coherent magnetization change and a clearer magnetic phase transition.
Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will have a smaller magnetic hysteresis-loop area.
Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will have a sharper and enhanced magnetocaloric response under low applied fields.
The as-deposited baseline exhibits significant hysteresis and a subdued magnetocaloric response because of strain- and defect-induced domain-wall pinning.
The annealing effect should be most pronounced in nanoscale films and patterned nanoribbons under low applied fields.
Heat-transfer rate limits the achievable magnetic-cooling cycle frequency in the stated operating regime.
Measurements should be performed near the alloy's magnetic-transition temperature under steady-state heat-exchange conditions.
The comparison should use identically cycled as-deposited and annealed samples and measure entropy change, refrigerant capacity, hysteresis, coercivity, lattice strain, and defect density.
Failure to observe reduced hysteresis or enhanced magnetocaloric response after annealing is stated to falsify the proposed mechanism.
